t: Distinct Points Reachable After Substring Removal — Prefix Sums
o: Removing one length-k block from s leaves a prefix plus a suffix; the final coordinate is the total displacement minus the displacement of the removed block. Precomputing prefix displacements lets us evaluate every removal start in O(1) and collect results in a set. In example 1, removing each single character gives displacements (-1,1), (-2,0), (-1,1) → 2 distinct points. Constraints (n ≤ 1e5) rule out recomputing each window from scratch in the worst case, motivating prefix sums.
k: Final position after removing s[i..i+k) = total displacement − (prefix[i+k] − prefix[i]).
A hash set of coordinate pairs deduplicates answers in O(n) overall.

a.i: For each of the n−k+1 removal positions, walk the remaining moves directly and record the endpoint. Simple and clearly correct, but O(n·k) time.
s: For each start i, iterate all characters except s[i..i+k), accumulating dx, dy.
a.t: O(n·k) — each of up to n windows rescans the string
a.sp: O(n) for the set of endpoints

a.i: Store cumulative (x, y) after each character. The displacement of any substring is a difference of two prefixes, so each removal is evaluated in O(1).
s: Build prefix arrays px, py with px[0]=py[0]=0.
Total = (px[n], py[n]). For each start i, subtract prefix difference over [i, i+k).
Insert encoded coordinate into a hash set and return its size.
a.t: O(n) — one prefix pass plus one set pass
a.sp: O(n) — prefix arrays and the set

w: Always present the prefix-sum solution in interviews; brute force is only a stepping stone. Pitfalls: forgetting k = n (empty remainder ends at origin), and encoding coordinates safely in hash sets in single-value languages. Follow-ups: count distinct points when removing a substring of any length, or removal of exactly two substrings.
